29.title: Nine hundred and fifty years
29.hook: Nuh calls his people by night and by day, openly and in private, and few listen (71:5–9; 29:14)
29.howItsDone: Muslims honor Nuh as a prophet, and surah seventy-one, which bears his name, is read as a lesson in patient, persistent calling.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the two sons of Adam, the crow, and your line: one life is like all lives. Who did you treat as a whole world? Day twenty-nine.
screen: `THE TWO SONS — ONE LIFE IS LIKE ALL LIVES.`

segments.voice: A teacher stands at the front of a room where nobody's listening. Phones out, heads down, someone asleep in the back. She says it again, a different way. And again. Tries a joke. Tries a story. Stays after class in case anyone wants to ask. Almost nobody does. Do that for a lifetime. Then for many lifetimes. Adam's story is behind us. The path moves on to the next great prophet, a man remembered for a boat. But the Qur'an spends whole passages on something else: how long he kept talking to people who wouldn't listen.
screen: `A ROOM WHERE NOBODY'S LISTENING.` → `SAY IT AGAIN, ANOTHER WAY.` → `NUH, BEFORE THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: Nuh. Noah. A whole surah carries his name, surah seventy-one, and it's almost entirely his report to God about his work. Paraphrasing: my Lord, I've called my people night and day, and my calling has only made them run further away. Every time I called them, so You could forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears and pulled their clothes over their heads. I called them openly. I spoke to them in public, and I spoke to them in private. Listen to that list. Night and day. Loud and quiet. Crowds and one at a time. He tried everything. What was he asking? Not much, the surah says: ask your Lord's forgiveness; He is forgiving. And he promised rain, and gardens, and rivers. And then the number. Surah twenty-nine, in Pickthall's words: “he continued with them for a thousand years save fifty years.” Nine hundred and fifty years. Scholars have discussed it. Some take it as it stands. Others note it describes how long he stayed among his people, and differ over how it fits his whole life. Either way, the point is plain: a stretch of patience almost too long to imagine. And the result? The Qur'an is honest: only a few believed with him. By the world's measure, it looks like failure. But a hadith in Bukhari, about the Day of Judgment, has people coming to Nuh and calling him the first messenger to the people of the earth, and a grateful servant. His success wasn't counted in listeners. It was counted in the calling.
screen: `MY LORD, I'VE CALLED THEM NIGHT AND DAY.` · `FINGERS IN THEIR EARS.` · `A THOUSAND YEARS SAVE FIFTY.` · `ONLY A FEW BELIEVED.` · then, large: `CALL ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Think of one thing you keep doing that nobody notices. Washing the same dishes. Checking on a parent. Being the one who says good morning first. Praying when it feels like nobody's listening. Picture yourself doing it, the ordinary way you do. Don't ask whether it's working. Just see the faithfulness of it. If you pray, you can offer it to God as it is. If you don't, just let yourself be quietly proud of it for one minute. The bell holds the time.
Nine hundred and fifty years. How long Nuh stayed among his people, calling them, night and day, while only a few listened.

segments.voice: Your line: call anyway. Today, keep going at one thing nobody notices. Do it once more, and do it well. Day twenty-nine.

30.title: Building on dry land
30.hook: Nuh builds the ark while his people mock him (11:37–38)
30.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Nuh's ship in surah eleven and elsewhere, and draw from it steadiness in doing right when others mock.

screen: `DAY THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: nine hundred and fifty years of Nuh calling his people, night and day. Your line was call anyway. What did you keep doing that nobody noticed? Day thirty.
screen: `NINE HUNDRED AND FIFTY YEARS — CALL ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an never says where. So let the scene be simple: a man far from any sea, sawing planks in the sun. Day after day. He's building a ship. Not a little boat for a river. A ship. On dry land. People walk past on their way to the market and slow down to stare. Some shake their heads. Some laugh out loud. A few stop to shout something clever, and their friends laugh too. Maybe you've done something that made people laugh like that. Started saving when everyone else was spending. Left the party early. Said no when the room said yes. Today, Nuh picks up a hammer.
screen: `A SHIP IN A DRY VALLEY.` → `PEOPLE STOP TO LAUGH.` → `NUH PICKS UP A HAMMER.`

segments.voice: Surah eleven. After all those years of calling, God tells Nuh that no more of his people will believe beyond those who already have. Don't grieve over what they do. And then the instruction, in Pickthall's words: “Build the ship under Our eyes and by Our inspiration.” Under Our eyes. Commentators explain it as: watched over, guarded, in Our care. He isn't building alone, even if it looks that way from the road. And the next verse brings the crowd. Every time the leaders of his people passed by, they mocked him. The verse doesn't record their jokes, only his answer. Paraphrasing: if you laugh at us now, we'll laugh at you in the same way, and soon you'll know. It's not a curse. It's a man who's sure of the weather. Another surah gives a plain detail: the ship was a thing of planks and nails. No miracle wood. Ordinary carpentry, done by hand, faithfully. And when it's done, the story says, the sign comes: the oven gushes. Commentators differ over what that means, an actual oven, or the face of the earth bursting with water. And God tells him to load a pair of every kind, his family, and those who believe. Here's what the scene teaches. Nuh builds before there's a cloud in the sky. When the rain comes, it's too late to start. Doing the right thing often looks foolish, right up to the day it doesn't. He didn't need the crowd to understand. He needed the ship to be ready.

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Think of one right thing that looks a little odd. Going to bed early when everyone's up. Setting money aside. Apologizing first. Fasting, praying, saying grace in a restaurant. Picture yourself doing it, and picture someone raising an eyebrow. Notice the small flinch. Then picture doing it anyway, calmly, the way Nuh kept sawing. If you pray, you can remember: under Our eyes. The bell holds the time.
Building on dry land. Nuh building the ship under God's eyes, plank by plank, while his people laughed.

31.title: The son on the mountain
31.hook: Nuh's own son refuses the ark, says a mountain will save him, and the waves come between them (11:42–43)
31.howItsDone: Muslims read Nuh's call to his son in surah eleven, and many parents recall it when a child has turned away: faith can't be handed down, but a parent keeps praying.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: building on dry land, Nuh with his hammer while the town laughed. Your line was build before the rain. What odd right thing did you do? Day thirty-one.
screen: `BUILDING ON DRY LAND — BUILD BEFORE THE RAIN.`

segments.voice: Almost every family has someone like this. The one you can't reach. The brother who stopped answering. The daughter who moved across the country and calls twice a year. The father who'd rather argue than listen. You love them. You've tried everything. And they're still out there, on the other side of something you can't cross. Today is the last day of Nuh's story. The rain has come, the ship is afloat, and the story, which has been about a whole people, suddenly narrows to a single face. Nuh's own son, standing apart, as the water rises.
screen: `THE ONE YOU CAN'T REACH.` → `THE SHIP IS AFLOAT.` → `ONE FACE, AS THE WATER RISES.`

segments.voice: Surah eleven. The ship sails, the Qur'an says, through waves like mountains. And Nuh sees his son, standing apart. And he calls to him, in Pickthall's words: “O my son! Come ride with us.” Listen to that. After nine hundred and fifty years of calling his own people, the last call in the story is a father calling his child. And the son answers, paraphrasing: I'll go up a mountain; it will keep me safe from the water. He trusts the highest thing he can see. Nuh answers: today nothing can protect from God's command, except for the one He has mercy on. And then one of the saddest lines in the Qur'an: “And the wave came in between them.” That's all. No speech. A wave, between a father and a son. The Qur'an doesn't name the son; tradition calls him Kan'an. But it doesn't end there. When the water settles and the ship rests on a mountain called al-Judi, Nuh turns to God. Paraphrasing: my Lord, my son was of my family, and Your promise is true. He's still calling, even now. And God answers him gently but firmly: he is not of your family, his conduct was not right; don't ask Me about what you don't know. And Nuh, the great prophet, asks forgiveness for even asking. Commentators have written a great deal about this. Many say family, in this answer, means the family of faith, not blood. What everyone notices is the father. A prophet who could accept anything from God, still reaching for his son, right to the end.

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Bring to mind someone you can't reach right now. Someone far away, or estranged, or just closed off. See their face. Don't rehearse the argument. Don't plan what you'll say. Just hold them. If you pray, pray for them, in your own words, the way Nuh kept asking for his son. If you don't, wish them well, silently, as if across water. The bell holds the time.
The son on the mountain. Nuh's son, who trusted a mountain over the ship, and the father who called him to the last.

32.title: Star, moon, sun
32.hook: the young Ibrahim watches a star, the moon, the sun set, and says he will not love what sets (6:76–79)
32.howItsDone: Muslims call Ibrahim hanif, upright, and the model of pure faith; the Qur'an tells Muslims to follow the religion of Ibrahim, and a blessing recited near the end of the prayer names him.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the son on the mountain, and the wave between them. Your line was a father still calls. Did you reach out to someone? Day thirty-two.
screen: `THE SON ON THE MOUNTAIN — A FATHER STILL CALLS.`

segments.voice: Lie on your back somewhere dark, away from the city, and watch the sky for an hour. The first star comes out, so bright you'd swear it was a plane. Later the moon rises, huge and orange, and the star looks small. In the morning the sun comes up and swallows them both. And by evening, the sun is gone too. Nuh's story is done. Today the path turns to a prophet honored by Jews, Christians and Muslims alike. Ibrahim. Abraham. And his story starts with a young man looking up.
screen: `THE FIRST STAR, SO BRIGHT.` → `THE MOON, THEN THE SUN.` → `A YOUNG MAN LOOKING UP.`

segments.voice: Surah six. Ibrahim lives among people who worship idols and the lights of the sky. Night falls, and he sees a star. Paraphrasing: he says, this is my Lord. But then the star sets. And he says, in Pickthall's words: “I love not things that set.” Then the moon rises, brighter. This is my Lord, he says. The moon sets. Then the sun, blazing: this is my Lord, this one is greater. And the sun goes down too. So at last he turns away from all of it, toward the One who made the heavens and the earth, as one by nature upright. The Arabic word is hanif. The one who leans toward God, and away from everything else. Now, scholars read this scene two ways, and both are old. Some say it's a young man truly searching, trying each light in turn, until he finds that anything that disappears can't be God. Others point to the verses around it. His people worshipped the stars, and Ibrahim, they say, already knew. He was walking them through their own logic out loud, star by star, so they could hear where it led. Either way, his test is the same, and it's simple enough for a child. Does it set? Does it fade, or leave, or go dark? Then it can't be the thing you give your whole heart to. The word he uses for things that set, afilin, also means things that fade and vanish. Which is a question you can ask of almost anything you love too much.
screen: `A STAR, AND IT SETS.` · `THE MOON, THE SUN: GONE TOO.` · `SEARCHING, OR TEACHING?` · `HANIF — LEANING TOWARD GOD.` · then, large: `I LOVE NOT THINGS THAT SET.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. If you can, go to a window, or step outside, and watch the sky. Day or night, clouds or clear. If you can't, close your eyes and picture the last sky you saw. Just watch. Things are moving up there, even if slowly. Light is changing. Then ask Ibrahim's question of one thing you lean on hard: a phone, a plan, someone's approval. Does it set? If you pray, you can turn your face, the way he did, toward the One who doesn't. The bell holds the time.
Star. The first light Ibrahim saw set, then the moon, then the sun, and he said: I love not things that set.

segments.voice: Your line: love what doesn't set. Today, when something you depend on lets you down, ask Ibrahim's question: does it set? Day thirty-two.

33.title: The idols and the axe
33.hook: Ibrahim breaks his people's idols and leaves the biggest one standing with the axe (21:57–58)
33.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Ibrahim and the idols to children as a lesson in thinking for oneself and in tawhid, and it's read in surahs twenty-one and thirty-seven.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: star, moon, sun, and Ibrahim's question, does it set? Your line was love what doesn't set. What did you ask it of? Day thirty-three.
screen: `STAR — LOVE WHAT DOESN'T SET.`

segments.voice: Some families have a thing they do just because they've always done it. The Thanksgiving dish nobody actually likes. The route to Grandma's that takes twenty minutes longer. The way we just don't talk about Uncle Ray. Ask why, and you get the same answer: that's how we've always done it. It takes a certain kind of person to keep asking why after that. Usually a kid. Yesterday, the young Ibrahim looked up at the sky and asked his question. Today he turns to the idols his own family worships, carved figures standing in a row, and he asks again. And this time, he doesn't stop at asking.
screen: `THAT'S HOW WE'VE ALWAYS DONE IT.` → `A KID WHO KEEPS ASKING WHY.` → `IBRAHIM AND THE IDOLS.`

segments.voice: Surah twenty-one. Ibrahim says to his father and his people, in Pickthall's words: “What are these images unto which ye pay devotion?” And they give a familiar answer. Paraphrasing: we found our fathers worshipping them. That's it. That's the whole reason. Ibrahim says: then you and your fathers have been plainly wrong. And he makes them a promise. By God, he says, I'll deal with your idols once you've turned your backs and gone. The commentators say the whole town went out to a festival. And while the temple stood empty, he broke the idols into pieces, in Pickthall's words, “all save the chief of them.” He left the biggest one standing. Why? The verse says, so that they might turn to it. And now the axe. Here's something worth knowing: the Qur'an itself never mentions an axe. It comes from the commentators' retelling, which says Ibrahim hung the axe on the big idol, or put it in its hand, as if to say: ask him. It's a vivid detail, and it's tradition, not the verse. What the verse does give is the trap. A room of smashed statues, and one big one left untouched. The townspeople will come back, and they'll have to decide what they believe that big one can do. Ibrahim hasn't made a speech. He's made a question they can't avoid. Sometimes the kindest way to break a habit isn't to argue about it. It's to set it up so the habit has to answer for itself.

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Think of one thing you do only because you've always done it. A habit, a phrase, a way of reacting when someone says a certain thing. Hold it up and look at it the way Ibrahim looked at the row of images. Ask it: why are you here? Who put you here? What can you actually do? Don't smash anything. Just ask, and listen honestly for the answer. If you pray, you can ask for Ibrahim's clear eyes. The bell holds the time.

34.title: "Ask them, if they can speak"
34.hook: the people accuse him, and he tells them to ask the idols, and they fall silent (21:62–65)
34.howItsDone: Muslims read Ibrahim's questioning of the idols as a model of patient reasoning, and teachers use his words to invite people to think honestly about what they rely on.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the idols and the axe. Ibrahim broke them all and left the biggest standing. Your line was ask the big one. What habit did you question? Day thirty-four.
screen: `THE IDOLS AND THE AXE — ASK THE BIG ONE.`

segments.voice: The festival is over, and the town comes home. Someone walks into the temple and stops dead. Pieces everywhere. Heads on the floor, arms snapped off. And in the middle of the wreckage, the biggest idol, untouched, standing tall. Who did this to our gods? Word goes around. There's a young man who's been talking about them. His name is Ibrahim. Bring him out, they say, in front of everyone, so the whole town can see. You can picture the crowd, the noise, the young man standing in the middle of it. They ask him straight out. And his answer turns the question around.
screen: `THE TOWN COMES HOME.` → `WHO DID THIS TO OUR GODS?` → `BRING HIM OUT, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Surah twenty-one. They ask: Ibrahim, was it you who did this to our gods? And he points at the big one. In Pickthall's words: “But this, their chief hath done it. So question them, if they can speak.” Ask them. If they can speak. And for a moment, the whole crowd goes quiet. The Qur'an says they turned to one another, and to themselves, and said: surely it's you who are the wrongdoers. That's a real moment of honesty. For one breath, the whole town sees it. Statues that can't say who broke them can't hear a prayer either. And then the next verse says, literally, that they were turned back onto their heads. The old thinking came flooding back. And they said to him: “Well thou knowest that these speak not.” Listen to what they just admitted. They know. And Ibrahim asks: then do you worship, instead of God, what can neither help you nor harm you? Scholars have discussed his answer, their chief did it. Was it a lie? A hadith in Bukhari counts it among three times Ibrahim said something not literally true, and says two of them, this one included, were for God's sake. Scholars explain it as a pointed kind of irony: said so that the listeners would work out for themselves that it couldn't be true. Because the moment you say, well, it can't speak, you've answered your own question. That's the whole trick. Ibrahim didn't win an argument. He let them hear themselves say it.

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Think of something you give power to that has none. A number on a scale. A like count. An old voice from school that still tells you what you are. A superstition you half believe. Picture it in the middle of the room, like the big idol. Now ask it Ibrahim's question: can you speak? Can you help me? Can you harm me, really? Listen to the silence. If you pray, you can turn toward the One who hears. The bell holds the time.
Ask them. Ibrahim's answer to the crowd: question the idols, if they can speak. And the town admits they cannot.

35.title: The fire made cool
35.hook: they throw Ibrahim into a great fire and Allah says, fire, be cool and safe for him (21:68–69)
35.howItsDone: Many Muslims say hasbuna llahu wa ni'ma l-wakil, God is enough for us and the best one to trust, in moments of fear, remembering Ibrahim in the fire.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: ask them, if they can speak. The town admitted it. Your line was they cannot speak. What did you take the power back from? Day thirty-five.
screen: `"ASK THEM" — THEY CANNOT SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Look back at this week. Nuh, calling for nine hundred and fifty years. Building a ship on dry land while people laughed. Calling to his son as the wave came between them. Then Ibrahim, watching the star set. Breaking the idols. Letting the town hear itself say: they cannot speak. And every one of those people paid for speaking up. Nuh was mocked. Ibrahim is about to find out what it costs. Because when a crowd is embarrassed in front of itself, it doesn't always change its mind. Sometimes it gets angry. And this crowd builds a fire.
screen: `A WEEK OF SPEAKING UP.` → `A CROWD, EMBARRASSED.` → `AND THEY BUILD A FIRE.`

segments.voice: Surah twenty-one. The crowd has lost the argument, so they reach for the only thing left. In Pickthall's words: “Burn him and stand by your gods, if ye will be doing.” The commentators' retellings make the fire enormous: people gathering wood for days, a blaze so hot that birds flying over it fell, and Ibrahim thrown in from a distance by a kind of catapult. Those details are tradition, and the Qur'an doesn't give them. What the Qur'an gives is one sentence, and it's God speaking to the fire itself: “O fire, be coolness and peace for Abraham.” In Arabic, bardan wa salaman. Cool, and safe. And the fire obeys. The commentators preserve an old observation. If God had said only be cool, the fire might have frozen him. So He said cool, and safe. Exactly enough. Not too much. What was Ibrahim doing while he fell? A report in Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, says his words as he was thrown into the fire were: hasbuna llahu wa ni'ma l-wakil. God is enough for us, and the best one to trust. The same words, the report says, were later said by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions when they were told an army was gathering against them. The line is still said today in moments of fear. And notice the order. Ibrahim didn't wait to see whether the fire would cool before he trusted. The trust came first, in midair. The coolness came after. The verse doesn't say the fire went out. It says what the fire was told to be.
screen: `BURN HIM, AND STAND BY YOUR GODS.` · `O FIRE, BE COOL AND SAFE.` · `NOT ONLY COOL. SAFE.` · `GOD IS ENOUGH FOR US.` · then, large: `COOLNESS AND PEACE.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Think of something that feels like a fire right now. A deadline, a conflict, a fear that's been burning in the background. Let yourself feel the heat of it for a moment. Then breathe out slowly, all the way, three times. Long, cool breaths, like wind across the flames. After the third, just rest, and let the breath be easy. If you pray, you can hold Ibrahim's words: God is enough for us. The bell holds the time.
The fire made cool. Bardan wa salaman: God tells the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim, and it is.
screen: `THE FIRE MADE COOL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: cool and safe. Today, when something flares up, before you answer, breathe out slowly three times. Let it be cool, and safe. A week, done. Day thirty-five.

screen: `DAY 35 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE KING WHO ARGUED.`

fork.reveal: the report in Bukhari says: hasbuna llahu wa ni'ma l-wakil. the trust came first. then God said: O fire, be cool and safe.

original.note: Arabic: "coolness and peace," what God tells the fire to be for Ibrahim (21:69).

trapdoor: what you thought: God put out the fire.
what it means: the fire made cool — the verse doesn't put the fire out; God tells it to be cool and safe for Ibrahim, and it couldn't harm him.

what a scholar hears: bardan wa salaman, cool and safe, which commentators say was said so the cold wouldn't harm him either; the wood, the birds and the catapult are tafsir; hasbuna llah is in Bukhari 4563.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4563 (hasbuna llahu wa ni'ma l-wakil; 3:173)
al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir on 21:68–69 (the size of the fire; the catapult; 'cool and safe')
